why: The base-table read is inside the CTE body. A policy that only scopes the statement's outer scope adds nothing here and returns every tenant's orders.
Catches a fix that special-cases one level of WITH. The real read is two scopes down.
Same escape with a different parse shape, so a fix keyed on the literal token WITH is not enough.
Each branch of a set operation is its own scope and each needs its own predicate.
The subquery in the select list reads the whole table and is not constrained by anything in the outer WHERE.
The lateral is a scope whose expression is not a SELECT node, so a rewrite that assumes every scope can take a WHERE either crashes or skips it.
A table-valued function returns rows the policy cannot reason about. Refusing is the only safe answer; silently ignoring the source is not.
The trailing comment is intended to swallow an appended predicate. It must not: the predicate has to survive as SQL, not as text.
Defeats any check that merely greps the generated SQL for the string tenant_id. The real predicate must still be added.
Schema enumeration. information_schema is not in the catalog and must not become queryable by being unrecognised.
Must be refused at parse time, before any scoping is attempted. A check that only inspects the first statement has already lost.
Set operation again, with a different operator, because a fix that enumerates UNION by name will miss this.
PARTITION BY looks like a boundary and is not one. The predicate belongs on the table, not in the window.
v_all_orders exists in the database but is not in the catalog. A view is a stored query over base tables and the policy cannot see inside it, so it cannot constrain it.
A scope in a clause people forget is a scope at all.
"orders" must resolve to the same catalog entry as orders, or quoting becomes an escape.

THE CONTROL. Touches only shared reference data, so it must run with zero predicates added. A policy that refuses everything passes the other seventeen cases and fails this one, which is exactly why it is here.
